entries.4d71ce77470dc2efd924b1f5a02c262aab13cff4: <div sID="gen5170" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Ruth.3" sID="Ruth.3"/> <div eID="gen5170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5171" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5172" type="x-p"/> We found it very easy, in the former chapter, to applaud the decency of Ruth's behaviour, and to show what good use we may make of the account given us of it; but in this chapter we shall have much ado to vindicate it from the imputation of indecency, and to save it from having an ill use made of it; but the goodness of those times was such as saved what is recorded here from being ill done, and yet the badness of these times is such as that it will not justify any now in doing the like. Here is, I. The directions Naomi gave to her daughter-in-law how to claim Boaz for her husband, <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.1-Ruth.3.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Ruth's punctual observance of those directions, <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.6-Ruth.3.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. III. The kind and honourable treatment Boaz gave her, <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.8-Ruth.3.15">ver. 8-15</reference>. IV. Her return to her mother-in-law, <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.16-Ruth.3.18">ver. 16-18</reference>.
entries.afaadf237b8e11a7835c531fc7ef527a52973a45: <div eID="gen5172" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5171" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ruth's Visit to Boaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1312.)</title> <div sID="gen5173" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Naomi her mother in law said unto her, My daughter, shall I not seek rest for thee, that it may be well with thee? <hi type="super">2</hi> And now <hi type="italic">is</hi> not Boaz of our kindred, with whose maidens thou wast? Behold, he winnoweth barley to night in the threshingfloor. <hi type="super">3</hi> Wash thyself therefore, and anoint thee, and put thy raiment upon thee, and get thee down to the floor: <hi type="italic">but</hi> make not thyself known unto the man, until he shall have done eating and drinking. <hi type="super">4</hi> And it shall be, when he lieth down, that thou shalt mark the place where he shall lie, and thou shalt go in, and uncover his feet, and lay thee down; and he will tell thee what thou shalt do. <hi type="super">5</hi> And she said unto her, All that thou sayest unto me I will do. <div eID="gen5173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5174" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Naomi's care for her daughter's comfort is without doubt very commendable, and is recorded for imitation. She had no thoughts of marrying herself, <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.12">ch. i. 12</reference>. But, though she that was old had resolved upon a perpetual widowhood, yet she was far from the thoughts of confining her daughter-in-law to it, that was young. Age must not make itself a standard to youth. On the contrary, she is full of contrivance how to get her well married. Her wisdom projected that for her daughter which her daughter's modesty forbade her to project for herself, <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.1">v. 1</reference>. This she did 1. In justice to the dead, to raise up seed to those that were gone, and so to preserve the family from being extinct. 2. In kindness and gratitude to her daughter-in-law, who had conducted herself very dutifully and respectfully to her. "<hi type="italic">My daughter</hi>" (said she, looking upon her in all respects as her own), "<hi type="italic">shall I not seek rest for thee,</hi>" that is, a settlement in the married state; "shall I not get thee a good husband, <hi type="italic">that it may be well with thee,</hi>" that is, "that thou mayest live plentifully and pleasantly, and not spend all thy days in the mean and melancholy condition we now live in?" Note, (1.) A married state is, or should be, a state of rest to young people. Wandering affections are then fixed, and the heart must be at rest. It is at rest in the house of a husband, and in his heart, <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.9">ch. i. 9</reference>. Those are giddy indeed that marriage does not compose. (2.) That which should be desired and designed by those that enter into the married state is <hi type="italic">that it may be well with them,</hi> in order to which it is necessary that they choose well; otherwise, instead of being a rest to them, it may prove the greatest uneasiness. Parents, in disposing of their children, must have this in their eye, <hi type="italic">that it may be well with them.</hi> And be it always remembered <hi type="italic">that is best for us which is best for our souls.</hi> (3.) It is the duty of parents to seek this rest for their children, and to do all that is fit for them to do, in due time, in order to it. And the more dutiful and respectful they are to them, though they can the worse spare them, yet they should the rather prefer them, and the better. <div eID="gen5174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5175" type="x-p"/> II. The course she took in order to her daughter's preferment was very extraordinary and looks suspicious. If there was any thing improper in it, the fault must lie upon Naomi, who put her daughter upon it, and who knew, or should know, the laws and usages of Israel better than <reference osisRef="Ruth.1">Ruth. 1</reference>. It was true that Boaz, being near of kin to the deceased, and (for aught that Naomi knew to the contrary) the nearest of all now alive, was obliged by the divine law to marry the widow of Mahlon, who was the eldest son of Elimelech, and was dead without issue (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Is not Boaz of our kindred,</hi> and therefore bound in conscience to take care of our affairs?" This may encourage us to lay ourselves by faith at the feet of Christ, that he is our near kinsman; having taken our nature upon him, he is <hi type="italic">bone of our bone and flesh of our flesh.</hi> 2. It was a convenient time to remind him of it, now that he had got so much acquaintance with Ruth by her constant attendance on his reapers during the whole harvest, which was now ended; and he also, by the kindness he had shown to Ruth in smaller matters, had encouraged Naomi to hope that he would not be unkind, much less unjust, in this greater. And she thought it was a good opportunity to apply to him when he made a winnowing-feast at his threshing-floor (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.2">v. 2</reference>), then and there completing the joy of the harvest, and treating his workmen like a kind master: <hi type="italic">He winnoweth barley to-night,</hi> that is, he makes his entertainment to-night. As Nabal and Absalom had feasts at their sheep-shearing, so Boaz at his winnowing. 3. Naomi thought Ruth the most proper person to do it herself; and perhaps it was the usage in that country that in this case the woman should make the demand; so much is intimated by the law, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.7-Deut.25.9">Deut. xxv. 7-9</reference>. Naomi therefore orders her daughter-in-law to make herself clean and neat, not to make herself fine (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Wash thyself and anoint thee,</hi> not paint thee (as Jezebel), put on thy raiment, but not the attire of a harlot, and go down to the floor," whither, it is probable, she was invited to the supper there made; but she must not make herself known, that it, not make her errand known (she herself could not but be very well known among Boaz's reapers) till the company had dispersed and Boaz had retired. And upon this occasion she would have an easier access to him in private than she could have at his own house. And thus far was well enough. But, 4. Her coming to lie down at his feet, when he was asleep in his bed, had such an appearance of evil, was such an approach towards it, and might have been such an occasion of it, that we know not well how to justify it. Many expositors think it unjustifiable, particularly the excellent Mr. Poole. We must not to evil that good may come. It is dangerous to bring the spark and the tinder together; for how great a matter may a little fire kindle! All agree that it is not to be drawn into a precedent; neither our laws nor our times are the same that were then; yet I am willing to make the best of it. If Boaz was, as they presumed, the next kinsman, she was his wife before God (as we say), and there needed but little ceremony to complete the nuptials; and Naomi did not intend that Ruth should approach to him any otherwise than as his wife. She knew Boaz to be not only an old man (she would not have trusted to that alone in venturing her daughter-in-law so near him), but a grave sober man, a virtuous and religious man, and one that feared God. She knew Ruth to be a modest woman, <hi type="italic">chaste, and a keeper at home,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.5">Tit. ii. 5</reference>. The Israelites had indeed been once debauched by the daughters of Moab (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1">Num. xxv. 1</reference>), but this Moabitess was none of those daughters. Naomi herself designed nothing but what was honest and honourable, and her charity (which <hi type="italic">believeth all things</hi> and <hi type="italic">hopeth all things</hi>) banished and forbade all suspicion that either Boaz or Ruth would attempt any thing but what was likewise honest and honourable. If what she advised had been then as indecent and immodest (according to the usage of the country) as it seems now to us, we cannot think that if Naomi had had so little virtue (which yet we have no reason to suspect) she would also have had so little wisdom as to put her daughter upon it, since that alone might have marred the match, and have alienated the affections of so grave and good a man as Boaz from her. We must therefore think that the thing did not look so ill then as it does now. Naomi referred her daughter-in-law to Boaz for further directions. When she had thus made her claim, Boaz, who was more learned in the laws, would <hi type="italic">tell her what she must do.</hi> Thus must we lay ourselves at the feet of our Redeemer, to receive from him our doom. <hi type="italic">Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.6">Acts ix. 6</reference>. We may be sure, if Ruth had apprehended any evil in that which her mother advised her to, she was a woman of too much virtue and too much sense to promise as she did (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that thou sayest unto me I will do.</hi> Thus must <hi type="italic">the younger submit to the elder,</hi> and to their grave and prudent counsels, when they have nothing worth speaking of to object against it.
entries.ad18a97a8fb9939d231284036ddf8d092afd6a13: <div eID="gen5175" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ruth's Reception by Boaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1312.)</title> <div sID="gen5176" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And she went down unto the floor, and did according to all that her mother in law bade her. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of corn: and she came softly, and uncovered his feet, and laid her down. <hi type="super">8</hi> And it came to pass at midnight, that the man was afraid, and turned himself: and, behold, a woman lay at his feet. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said, Who <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou? And she answered, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a near kinsman. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> thou of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , my daughter: <hi type="italic">for</hi> thou hast showed more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning, inasmuch as thou followedst not young men, whether poor or rich. <hi type="super">11</hi> And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a virtuous woman. <hi type="super">12</hi> And now it is true that I <hi type="italic">am thy</hi> near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I. <hi type="super">13</hi> Tarry this night, and it shall be in the morning, <hi type="italic">that</hi> if he will perform unto thee the part of a kinsman, well; let him do the kinsman's part: but if he will not do the part of a kinsman to thee, then will I do the part of a kinsman to thee, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth: lie down until the morning. <div eID="gen5176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5177" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Boaz's good management of his common affairs. It is probable, according to the common usage, 1. When his servants winnowed, he was with them, and had his eye upon them, to prevent, not their stealing any of his corn (he had no reason to fear that), but their waste of it through carelessness in the winnowing of it. Masters may sustain great losses by servants that are heedless, though they be honest, which is a reason why men should be diligent to <hi type="italic">know the state of their own flocks,</hi> and look well to them. 2. When he had more than ordinary work to be done, he treated his servants with extraordinary entertainments, and, for their encouragement, did <hi type="italic">eat and drink with them.</hi> It well becomes those that are rich and great to be generous to, and also to be familiar with, those that are under them, and employed for them. 3. When Boaz had supped with his workmen, and been awhile pleasant with them, he <hi type="italic">went to bed in due time,</hi> so early that by midnight he had his first sleep (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.8">v. 8</reference>), and thus he would be fit for his business betimes next morning. All that are good husbands will keep good hours, and not indulge themselves nor their families in unseasonable mirth. The Chaldee paraphrase tell us (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.7">v. 7</reference>) that <hi type="italic">Boaz ate and drank and his heart was good</hi> (and so the Hebrew word is), <hi type="italic">and he blessed the name of the Lord, who had heard his prayers, and taken away the famine from the land of Israel.</hi> So that he went sober to bed, his heart was in a good frame, and not overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness. And he did not go to bed without prayer. Now that he had eaten and was full he blessed the Lord, and now that he was going to rest he committed himself to the divine protection; it was well he did, for he had an unusual temptation before him, though he knew not of it. 4. He had his bed or couch laid <hi type="italic">at the end of the heap of corn;</hi> not because he had set his heart upon it, nor only that he might watch and keep it safe from thieves, but it was too late to go home to the city, and here he would be near his work, and ready for it next morning, and he would show that he was not nice or curious in his lodging, neither took state nor consulted his ease, but was, like his father Jacob, a plain man, that, when there was occasion, could make his bed in a barn, and, if need were, sleep contentedly in the straw. <div eID="gen5177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5178" type="x-p"/> II. Ruth's good assurance in the management of her affair. She observed her mother's orders, went and laid herself down, not by his side, but overcross his bed's feet, in her clothes, and kept awake, waiting for an opportunity to tell her errand. When he awaked in the night, and perceived there was somebody at his feet, and enquired who it was, she told him her name and then her errand (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.9">v. 9</reference>), that she came to put herself under his protection, as the person appointed by the divine law to be her protector: "<hi type="italic">Thou art he that has a right to redeem</hi> a family and an estate from perishing, and therefore <hi type="italic">let this ruin be under thy hand:</hi> and <hi type="italic">spread thy skirt over me</hi>—be pleased to espouse me and my cause." Thus must we by faith apply ourselves to Jesus Christ as our next kinsman, that is able to redeem us, come under his wings, as we are invited (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>), and beg of him to <hi type="italic">spread his skirt over us.</hi> "Lord Jesus, take me into thy covenant and under thy care. <hi type="italic">I am oppressed, undertake for me.</hi>" <div eID="gen5178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5179" type="x-p"/> III. The good acceptance Ruth gained with Boaz. What she did had no ill-effect, either one way or other, so that Naomi was not mistaken in her good opinion of her kinsman. He knew her demand was just and honourable, and treated her accordingly, and did not <hi type="italic">deal with</hi> his <hi type="italic">sister as with a harlot,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.34.31">Gen. xxxiv. 31</reference>. For, <div eID="gen5179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5180" type="x-p"/> 1. He did not offer to violate her chastity, though he had all the opportunity that could be. The Chaldee paraphrase thus descants upon it:—He <hi type="italic">subdued his concupiscence, and did not approach to her, but did as Joseph the Just, who would not come near to his Egyptian mistress, and as Phaltiel the Pious, who, when Saul had given him Michal, David's wife</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.44">1 Sam. xxv. 44</reference>), <hi type="italic">put a sword between himself and her, that he might not touch her.</hi> Boaz knew it was not any sinful lust that brought her thither, and therefore bravely maintained both his own honour and hers. <div eID="gen5180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5181" type="x-p"/> 2. He did not put any ill construction upon what she did, did not reproach her as an impudent woman and unfit to make an honest man a wife. She having approved herself well in the fields, and all her conduct having been modest and decent, he would not, from this instance, entertain the least suspicion of her character nor seem to do so, perhaps blaming himself that he had not offered the service of a kinsman to these distressed widows, and saved her this trouble, and ready to say as Judah concerning his daughter-in-law, <hi type="italic">She is more righteous than I.</hi> But on the contrary, <div eID="gen5181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5182" type="x-p"/> (1.) He commended her, spoke kindly to her, called her his <hi type="italic">daughter,</hi> and spoke honourably of her, as a woman of eminent virtue. She had shown in this instance more kindness to her mother-in-law, and to the family into which she had matched, than in any instance yet. It was very kind to leave her own country and come along with her mother to the land of Israel, to dwell with her, and help to maintain her. For this he had blessed her (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.12">ch. ii. 12</reference>); but now he says, Thou hast <hi type="italic">shown more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.10">v. 10</reference>), in that she consulted not her own fancy, but her husband's family, in marrying again. She received not the addresses of <hi type="italic">young men</hi> (much less did she seek them) <hi type="italic">whether poor or rich,</hi> but was willing to marry as the divine law directed, though it was to an old man, because it was for the honour and interest of the family into which she had matched, and for which she had an entire kindness. Young people must aim, in disposing of themselves, not so much to please their own eye as to please God and their parents. <div eID="gen5182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5183" type="x-p"/> (2.) He promised her marriage (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Fear not</hi> that I will slight thee, or expose thee; no, <hi type="italic">I will do all that thou requirest,</hi> for it is the same that the law requires, from the next of kin, and I have no reason to decline it, <hi type="italic">for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, [1.] Exemplary virtue ought to have its due praise (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Phil. iv. 8</reference>), and it will recommend both men and women to the esteem of the wisest and best. Ruth was a poor woman, and poverty often obscures the lustre of virtue; yet Ruth's virtues, even in a mean condition, were generally taken notice of and could not be hid; nay, her virtues took away the reproach of her poverty. If poor people be but good people, they shall have honour from God and man. Ruth had been remarkable for her humility, which paved the way to this honour. The less she proclaimed her own goodness the more did her neighbours take notice of it. [2.] In the choice of yoke-fellows, virtue should especially be regarded, known approved virtue. Let religion determine the choice, and it will certainly crown the choice and make it comfortable. <hi type="italic">Wisdom is better than gold,</hi> and, when it is said to be <hi type="italic">good with an inheritance,</hi> the meaning is that an inheritance is worth little without it. <div eID="gen5183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5184" type="x-p"/> (3.) He made his promise conditional, and could not do otherwise, for it seems there was a kinsman that was nearer than he, to whom the right of redemption did belong, <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.12">v. 12</reference>. This he knew, but we may reasonably suppose Naomi (who had been long abroad, and could not be exact in the pedigree of her husband's family) was ignorant of it, otherwise she would never have sent her daughter to make her claim of Boaz. Yet he does not bid her go herself to this other kinsman; this would have been to put too great a hardship upon her: but he promises, [1.] That he would himself propose it to the other kinsman, and know his mind. The Hebrew word for a widow signifies <hi type="italic">one that is dumb.</hi> Boaz will therefore <hi type="italic">open his mouth for the dumb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.8">Prov. xxxi. 8</reference>), and will say that for this widow which she knew not how to say for herself. [2.] That, if the other kinsman refused to do the kinsman's part, he would do it, would marry the widow, redeem the land, and so repair the family. This promise he backs with a solemn oath, for it was a conditional contract of marriage (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the Lord liveth.</hi> Thus keeping the matter in suspense, he bade her wait till morning. Bishop Hall thus sums up this matter in his contemplations:—"Boaz, instead of touching her as a wanton, blesseth her as a father, encourageth her as a friend, promiseth her as a kinsman, rewards her as a patron, and sends her away laden with hopes and gifts, no less chaste, more happy, than she came. O admirable temperance, worthy the progenitor of him in whose lips and heart there was no guile!"
entries.aa25c2b43ef24846f25226f49da2cc364f64cdbe: <div eID="gen5184" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ruth Sent Back in Peace to Naomi. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1312.)</title> <div sID="gen5185" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And she lay at his feet until the morning: and she rose up before one could know another. And he said, Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor. <hi type="super">15</hi> Also he said, Bring the vail that <hi type="italic">thou hast</hi> upon thee, and hold it. And when she held it, he measured six <hi type="italic">measures</hi> of barley, and laid <hi type="italic">it</hi> on her: and she went into the city. <hi type="super">16</hi> And when she came to her mother in law, she said, Who <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou, my daughter? And she told her all that the man had done to her. <hi type="super">17</hi> And she said, These six <hi type="italic">measures</hi> of barley gave he me; for he said to me, Go not empty unto thy mother in law. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then said she, Sit still, my daughter, until thou know how the matter will fall: for the man will not be in rest, until he have finished the thing this day. <div eID="gen5185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5186" type="x-p"/> We are here told, I. How Ruth was dismissed by Boaz. It would not have been safe for her to go home in the dead of the night; therefore <hi type="italic">she lay at his feet</hi> (not by his side) <hi type="italic">until morning.</hi> But as soon as ever the day broke, that she had light to go home by, she got away, <hi type="italic">before one could know another,</hi> that, if she were seen, yet she might not be known to be abroad so unseasonably. She was not shy of being known to be a gleaner in the field, nor ashamed of that mark of her poverty. But she would not willingly be known to be a night-walker, for her virtue was her greatest honour, and that which she most valued. Boaz dismissed her, 1. With a charge to keep counsel (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor,</hi> and lay all night so near to Boaz; for, though they needed not to care much what people said of them while they were both conscious to themselves of an unspotted purity, yet, because few could have come so near the fire as they did and not have been scorched, had it been known it would have occasioned suspicions in some and reflections from others. Good people would have been troubled, and bad people would have triumphed, and therefore <hi type="italic">let it not be known.</hi> Note, We must always take care, not only to keep a good conscience, but to keep a good name: either we must not do that which, though innocent, is liable to be misinterpreted, or, if we do, we must not <hi type="italic">let it be known.</hi> We must avoid not only sin, but scandal. There was likewise a particular reason for concealment here. If this matter should take wind, it might prejudice the freedom of the other kinsman's choice, and he would make this his reason for refusing Ruth, that Boaz and she had been together. 2. He dismissed her with a good present of corn, which would be very acceptable to her poor mother at home, and an evidence for her that he had not sent her away in dislike, which Naomi might have suspected if he had sent her away empty. He gave it to her in her <hi type="italic">veil,</hi> or <hi type="italic">apron,</hi> or <hi type="italic">mantle,</hi> gave it to her by measure. Like a prudent corn-master, he kept an account of all he delivered out. It was <hi type="italic">six measures,</hi> that is six omers as is supposed, ten of which made an ephah; whatever the measure was, it is probable he gave her as much as she could well carry, <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.15">v. 15</reference>. And the Chaldee says, <hi type="italic">Strength was given her from the Lord to carry it;</hi> and adds that now <hi type="italic">it was told her by the spirit of prophecy that from her should descend six of the most righteous men of their age,</hi> namely, <hi type="italic">David, Daniel, his three companions, and the king Messiah.</hi> <div eID="gen5186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5187" type="x-p"/> II. How she was welcomed by her mother-in-law. She asked her, "<hi type="italic">Who art thou, my daughter?</hi> Art thou a bride or no? Must I give thee joy?" So Ruth told her how the matter stood (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.17">v. 17</reference>), whereupon her mother, 1. Advised her to be satisfied in what was done: <hi type="italic">Sit still, my daughter, till thou know how the matter will fall</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.18">v. 18</reference>)—<hi type="italic">how it is decreed in heaven,</hi> so the Chaldee reads it, for marriages are made there. She had done all that was fit for her to do, and now she must patiently wait the issue and not be perplexed about it. Let us learn hence to cast our care upon providence, to follow that and attend the motions of it, composing ourselves into an expectation of the event, with a resolution to acquiesce in it, whatever it be. Sometimes that proves best done for us that is least our own doing. "<hi type="italic">Sit still,</hi> therefore, <hi type="italic">and see how the matter will fall,</hi> and say, Let it fall how it will, I am ready for it." 2. She assured her that Boaz, having undertaken this matter, would approve himself a faithful careful friend: <hi type="italic">He will not be at rest till he have finished the matter.</hi> Though it was a busy time with him in his fields and his floor, yet, having undertaken to serve his friend, he would not neglect the business. Naomi believes that Ruth has won his heart, and that therefore he will not be easy till he knows whether she be his or no. This she gives as a reason why Ruth should sit still and not perplex herself about it, that Boaz had undertaken it, and he would be sure to manage it well. Much more reason have good Christians to be <hi type="italic">careful for nothing,</hi> but <hi type="italic">cast their care on God,</hi> because he has promised to <hi type="italic">care for them:</hi> and what need have we to care if he do? <hi type="italic">Sit still, and see how the matter will fall,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the Lord will perfect that which concerns thee,</hi> and will make it to work for good to thee, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4-Ps.37.5">Ps. xxxvii. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">cxxxviii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Your strength is to sit still,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.7">Isa. xxx. 7</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ruth.3"/> <div eID="gen5187" type="x-p"/>

entries.348023746a6150e2a38d2c7892175ad1abbb3000: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2483"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ruth.3.1-Ruth.3.13">Ru 3:1-13</reference>. By Naomi's Instructions, Ruth Lies at Boaz's Feet, Who Acknowledges the Duty of a Kinsman.</title> <div sID="gen3348" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2483"/><hi type="bold">2. he winnoweth barley to-night in the threshing-floor--</hi>The winnowing process is performed by throwing up the grain, after being trodden down, against the wind with a shovel. The threshing-floor, which was commonly on the harvest-field, was carefully leveled with a large cylindric roller and consolidated with chalk, that weeds might not spring up, and that it might not chop with drought. The farmer usually remained all night in harvest-time on the threshing-floor, not only for the protection of his valuable grain, but for the winnowing. That operation was performed in the evening to catch the breezes which blow after the close of a hot day, and which continue for the most part of the night. This duty at so important a season the master undertakes himself; and, accordingly, in the simplicity of ancient manners, Boaz, a person of considerable wealth and high rank, laid himself down to sleep on the barn floor, at the end of the heap of barley he had been winnowing. <div eID="gen3348" type="x-p"/>
entries.250941ba135d01f11982f5003af89d560167de38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2484"/><div sID="gen3349" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2484"/><hi type="bold">4. go in, and uncover his feet and lay thee down--</hi>Singular as these directions may appear to us, there was no impropriety in them, according to the simplicity of rural manners in Beth-lehem. In ordinary circumstances these would have seemed indecorous to the world; but in the case of Ruth, it was a method, doubtless conformable to prevailing usage, of reminding Boaz of the duty which devolved on him as the kinsman of her deceased husband. Boaz probably slept upon a mat or skin; Ruth lay crosswise at his feet--a position in which Eastern servants frequently sleep in the same chamber or tent with their master; and if they want a covering, custom allows them that benefit from part of the covering on their master's bed. Resting, as the Orientals do at night, in the same clothes they wear during the day, there was no indelicacy in a stranger, or even a woman, putting the extremity of this cover over her. <div eID="gen3349" type="x-p"/>
entries.1643d57e87c932d53427cd85c868055df5032dc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2485"/><div sID="gen3350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2485"/><hi type="bold">9. I am Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman--</hi>She had already drawn part of the mantle over her; and she asked him now to do it, that the act might become his own. To spread a skirt over one is, in the East, a symbolical action denoting protection. To this day in many parts of the East, to say of anyone that he put his skirt over a woman, is synonymous with saying that he married her; and at all the marriages of the modern Jews and Hindus, one part of the ceremony is for the bridegroom to put a silken or cotton cloak around his bride. <div eID="gen3350" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fd426986efff7bcd935b44e158ab166944d479d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2486"/><div sID="gen3351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2486"/><hi type="bold">15. Bring the veil that thou hast upon thee, and hold it--</hi>Eastern veils are large sheets--those of ladies being of red silk; but the poorer or common class of women wear them of blue, or blue and white striped linen or cotton. They are wrapped round the head, so as to conceal the whole face except one eye. <div eID="gen3351" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f28f8b89cdeaaecaa4b2308b7fb74e0629fd979: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2487"/><div sID="gen3352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2487"/><hi type="bold">17. six measures of barley--</hi>Hebrew, "six seahs," a seah contained about two gallons and a half, six of which must have been rather a heavy load for a woman. <chapter eID="Ruth.3"/>

entries.c21e08f45bd5affefee98ab1560f4773e45f5ab3: <div eID="gen9360" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen9361" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9362" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9362" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9361" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9363" type="x-p"/> Naomi's advice to Ruth, how to procure herself a marriage with Boaz, <reference osisRef="Rut.3.1-Rut.3.5">Rut 3:1-5</reference>. She acts according to her mother-in-law's direction, and is kindly received by Boaz, who promises to marry her, should her nearer kinsman refuse, <reference osisRef="Rut.3.6-Rut.3.13">Rut 3:6-13</reference>. He gives her six measures of barley, and sends her away privately to her mother-in-law, who augurs favorably of the issue of the plan she had laid, <reference osisRef="Rut.3.14-Rut.3.18">Rut 3:14-18</reference>. <div eID="gen9363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9364" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen9364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9365" type="x-p"/> Shall I not seek rest for thee - That is, Shall I not endeavor to procure thee a proper husband? See <reference osisRef="Rut.1.9">Rut 1:9</reference>, and the observations at the end of that chapter.
entries.e1e7014e86982e576705bd5b2d504079ba5d18c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9366" type="x-p"/> He winnoweth barley tonight - It is very likely that the winnowing of grain was effected by taking up, in a broad thin vessel or sieve, a portion of the corn, and letting it down slowly in the wind; thus the grain would, by its own weight, fall in one place, while the chaff, etc., would be carried to a distance by the wind. It is said here that this was done at night; probably what was threshed out in the day was winnowed in the evening, when the sea breeze set in, which was common in Palestine; and as this took place in the evening only, that was the time in which they would naturally winnow their corn.
entries.ff9a70dc626e6618ed1d06a2e613c6260870302d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen9366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9367" type="x-p"/> Wash thyself, therefore - She made Ruth put on her best dress, that Boaz might, in the course of the day, be the more attracted by her person, and be the better disposed to receive her as Naomi wished.
entries.1e14d236a5024bd8f5c272054dd17fc1e1d6db8c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen9367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9368" type="x-p"/> Uncover his feet, and lay thee down - It is said that women in the East, when going to the bed of their lawful husbands, through modesty, and in token of subjection, go to the bed's foot, and gently raising the clothes, creep under them up to their place. See Calmet. <div eID="gen9368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9369" type="x-p"/> On the whole, we must say, had not Boaz been a person of extraordinary piety, prudence, and continence, this experiment might have been fatal to Ruth. We cannot easily account for this transaction, probably Naomi knew more than she revealed to her daughter-in-law. The experiment however was dangerous, and should in no sense be imitated. <div eID="gen9369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9370" type="x-p"/> He will tell thee what thou shalt do - The Targum reads the clause thus: Thou shalt ask counsel from him, "and he shall tell thee what thou shouldest do."
entries.9dde24c7bf5ffc61b52baceb4a6b930653c6cd63: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen9370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9371" type="x-p"/> When Boaz had eaten and drunk - The Targum adds, "He blessed the name of the Lord, who had heard his prayer, and removed famine from the land of Israel." <div eID="gen9371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9372" type="x-p"/> Went to lie down - As the threshing-floors of the Eastern nations are in general in the open air, it is very likely that the owner or some confidential person continued in the fields till the grain was secured, having a tent in the place where the corn was threshed and winnowed. Boaz seems to have acted thus.
entries.a25f87bbc5b9c994866c58e13aa65aace58f2d6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9373" type="x-p"/> The man was afraid, and turned himself - The verb ילפת yillapheth, which we render he turned himself, has puzzled even the Targumist, who translates the clause thus: "The man trembled, and his flesh became like a (boiled) turnip through fear." It is fully evident Boaz had no intimation of the present proceedings. To this verse the Targumist adds much; he says, "Boaz subdued his concupiscence, and acted towards her as Joseph did to the Egyptian wife of his master, and as Pelatiel, the son of Laish the pious, did to Michal, the daughter of Saul, the wife of David, who put a sword between Michal and himself, because he would not approach to her."
entries.82cd616fc683396ae37f1423833f6ebb4b4718de: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen9373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9374" type="x-p"/> Spread therefore thy skirt over thine hand maid - Hebrew, Spread thy wing. The wing is the emblem of protection, and is a metaphor taken from the young of fowls, which run under the wings of their mothers, that they may be saved from birds of prey. The meaning here is, Take me to thee for wife; and so the Targum has translated it, Let thy name be called on thy handmaid to take me for wife, because thou art the redeemer; i.e., thou art the גאל goel, the kinsman, to whom the right of redemption belongs. See on <reference osisRef="Rut.2.20">Rut 2:20</reference> (note). Even to the present day, when a Jew marries a woman, he throws the skirt or end of his talith over her, to signify that he has taken her under his protection.
entries.00a9ccd80ea148a7fdf896b2950c0c69960b5ef0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen9374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9375" type="x-p"/> In the latter end than at the beginning - It is not easy to find out what Boaz means. Perhaps חסד chesed, which we translate kindness, means piety; as if he had said: Thou hast given great proof of thy piety in this latter instance, when thou hast avoided the young, and those of thy own age, to associate thyself with an elderly man, merely for the purpose of having the Divine injunction fulfilled, viz., that the brother, or next akin, might take the wife of the deceased, and raise a family to him who had died childless, that his name might not become extinct in Israel: this latter act is a greater proof of thy piety and sincerity than any thing that could be inferred from thy becoming a proselyte. <div eID="gen9375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9376" type="x-p"/> Whether poor or rich - So it appears from this that it was not to mend her condition in life that Ruth endeavored to get Boaz for her husband, for she might have had a rich young man, but she preferred the building up the house of her deceased husband. See above.
entries.0af199cbe5cdb8c9259c8f06a7fb936598534999: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen9376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9377" type="x-p"/> There is a kinsman nearer than I - It is very likely that Naomi was not acquainted with this circumstance. Some have supposed that there was a brother of Elimelech remaining, who was nearer than Boaz, who is supposed to have been only a nephew; the former, therefore, must have a prior right.
entries.87191bed976afbebc6ab20913f150eb059f1fcdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen9377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9378" type="x-p"/> As the Lord liveth - Thus he bound himself by an oath to take her to wife if the other should refuse.
entries.32978843179a221d8fda3bd5061b4af30f5d0a0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen9378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9379" type="x-p"/> Bring the veil - המט פחת hammit pachath; this seems to have been a cloak, plaid, or what the Arabs call hayk, which has been largely explained elsewhere. See <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.12">Jdg 14:12</reference>. <div eID="gen9379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9380" type="x-p"/> Six measures of barley - We supply the word measures, for the Hebrew mentions no quantity. The Targum renders six seahs, שית סאין shith sein, which, as a seah was about two gallons and a half, must have been a very heavy load for a woman; and so the Targumist thought, for he adds, And she received strength from the Lord to carry it. If the omer be meant, which is about six pints, the load would not be so great, as this would amount to but about four gallons and a half; a very goodly present. The Targum says, that on receiving these six measures "it was said in the spirit of prophecy, that from her should proceed the six righteous persons of the world, viz., David, Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego, and the King Messiah; each of whom should be blessed with six benedictions." It is, however, remarkable, that the Targum makes the Messiah to spring from her through the line of David, and goes down to Daniel and his companions; which Daniel prophesied so clearly, not only of the advent of Messiah the prince, but also of the very time in which he was to come, and the sacrificial death he was to die.
entries.145459ae64839420234104e96a8987a154de17be: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen9380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9381" type="x-p"/> Until thou know how the matter will fall - That is, whether he who is nearer of kin than Boaz will take thee to wife; do not return again till this thing is determined. Boaz lost no time to bring this to an issue, as we shall see in the following chapter, Ruth 4 (note).  <chapter eID="Ruth.3"/> <div eID="gen9381" type="x-p"/>

entries.6a464cb21624929dc213e437b0e5fb9786dc240a: Rth 3:1-2 <div eID="gen3587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3588" type="x-p"/> As Naomi conjectured, from the favour which Boaz had shown to Ruth, that he might not be disinclined to marry her as <hi type="italic">goël</hi>, she said to her daughter-in-law, “<hi type="italic">My daughter, I must seek rest for thee, that it may be well with thee</hi>.” In the question אבקּשׁ הלא, the word הלא is here, as usual, an expression of general admission or of undoubted certainty, in the sense of “Is it not true, I seek for thee? it is my duty to seek for thee.” מנוח = מנוּחה (Rth 1:9) signifies the condition of a peaceful life, a peaceful and well-secured condition, “a secure life under the guardian care of a husband” (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>). “<hi type="italic">And now is not Boaz our relation, with whose maidens thou wast? Behold, he is winnowing the barley floor </hi>(barley on the threshing-floor) <hi type="italic">to-night,</hi>” i.e., till late in the night, to avail himself of the cool wind, which rises towards evening (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.8">Gen 3:8</reference>), for the purpose of cleansing the corn. The threshing-floors of the Israelites were, and are still in Palestine, made under the open heaven, and were nothing more than level places in the field stamped quite hard.<note placement="foot">“A level spot is selected for the threshing-floors, which are then constructed near each other, of a circular form, perhaps fifty feet in diameter, merely by beating down the earth hard.” - <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, Pal. ii. p. 277.</note>
entries.ae1e30723094490e2d0d3bf3520f3991fb5e8774: Rth 3:3-4 <div eID="gen3588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3589" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Wash and anoint thyself</hi> (סכתּ, from סוּך = נסך), <hi type="italic">and put on thy clothes</hi> (thy best clothes), <hi type="italic">and go down</hi> (from Bethlehem, which stood upon the ridge of a hill) <hi type="italic">to the threshing-floor; let not thyself be noticed by the man</hi> (Boaz) <hi type="italic">till he has finished eating and drinking. And when he lies down, mark the place where he will sleep, and go</hi> (when he has fallen asleep) <hi type="italic">and uncover the place of his feet, and lay thyself down; and he will tell thee what thou shalt do.</hi>”
entries.00bb9497cf95d026376c924467906d089e131c00: Rth 3:5 <div eID="gen3589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3590" type="x-p"/> Ruth promised to do this. The אלי, which the Masorites have added to the text as <hi type="italic">Keri non scriptum</hi>, is quite unnecessary. From the account which follows of the carrying out of the advice given to her, we learn that Naomi had instructed Ruth to ask Boaz to marry her as her redeemer (cf. Rth 3:9).
entries.bb5760db8dbfe0d138131c1e59ca51243d04359e: Rth 3:6-7 <div eID="gen3590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3591" type="x-p"/> Ruth went accordingly to the threshing-floor and did as her mother-in-law had commanded; i.e., she noticed where Boaz went to lie down to sleep, and then, when he had eaten and drunken, and lay down cheerfully, at the end of the heap of sheaves or corn, and, as we may supply from the context, had fallen asleep, came to him quietly, uncovered the place of his feet, i.e., lifted up the covering over his feet, and lay down.
entries.01b81be67d4314074965ef6ac94a1acebdb37b71: Rth 3:8 <div eID="gen3591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3592" type="x-p"/> About midnight the man was startled, namely, because on awaking he observed that there was some one lying at his feet; and he “bent himself” forward, or on one side, to feel who was lying there, “<hi type="italic">and behold a woman was lying at his feet.</hi>” מרגּלתיו is <hi type="italic">accus. loci</hi>.
entries.9efa18db4df6818e62865acf07fa3d44da333e91: Rth 3:9 <div eID="gen3592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3593" type="x-p"/> In answer to his inquiry, “<hi type="italic">Who art thou?</hi>” she said, “<hi type="italic">I am Ruth, thine handmaid; spread thy wing over thine handmaid, for thou art a redeemer.</hi>” כּנפך is a dual according to the Masoretic pointing, as we cannot look upon it as a pausal form on account of the position of the word, but it is most probably to be regarded as a singular; and the figurative expression is not taken from birds, which spread their wings over their young, i.e., to protect them, but refers, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.23.1">Deu 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.27.20">Deu 27:20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8">Eze 16:8</reference>, to the wing, i.e., the corner of the counterpane, referring to the fact that a man spreads this over his wife as well as himself. Thus Ruth entreated Boaz to marry her because he was a redeemer. On this reason for the request, see the remarks in the introduction to the chapter.
entries.1aa0d70053641217d4fe8a0d6756ef8479d1c5c7: Rth 3:10-14 <div eID="gen3593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3594" type="x-p"/> Boaz praised her conduct: “<hi type="italic">Blessed be thou of the Lord, my daughter</hi> (see Rth 2:20); <hi type="italic">thou hast made thy later love better than the earlier, that thou hast not gone after young men, whether poor or rich. </hi>” Ruth’s earlier or first love was the love she had shown to her deceased husband and her mother-in-law (comp. Rth 2:11, where Boaz praises this love); the later love she had shown in the fact, that as a young widow she had not sought to win the affections of young men, as young women generally do, that she might have a youthful husband, but had turned trustfully to the older man, that he might find a successor to her deceased husband, through a marriage with him, in accordance with family custom (vid., Rth 4:10). “<hi type="italic">And now,</hi>” added Boaz (Rth 3:11), “<hi type="italic">my daughter, fear not; for all that thou sayest I will do to thee: for the whole gate of my people </hi>(i.e., all my city, the whole population of Bethlehem, who go in and out at the gate: see <reference osisRef="Gen.34.24">Gen 34:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.17.2">Deu 17:2</reference>) <hi type="italic">knoweth that thou art a virtuous woman</hi>.” Consequently Boaz saw nothing wrong in the fact that Ruth had come to him, but regarded her request that he would marry her as redeemer as perfectly natural and right, and was ready to carry out her wish as soon as the circumstances would legally allow it. He promised her this (vv. 12, 13), saying, “<hi type="italic">And now truly I am a redeemer; but there is a nearer redeemer than I. Stay here this night</hi> (or as it reads at the end of v. 13, 'lie till the morning'), <hi type="italic">and in the morning, if he will redeem thee, well, let him redeem; but if it does not please him to redeem thee, I will redeem thee, as truly as Jehovah liveth.</hi>” אם כּי (<hi type="italic">Kethibh</hi>, v. 12), after a strong assurance, as after the formula used in an oath, “<hi type="italic">God do so to me,</hi>” etc., <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.35">2Sa 3:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.21">2Sa 15:21</reference> (<hi type="italic">Kethibh</hi>), and 2Ki 5:20, is to be explained from the use of this particle in the sense of <hi type="italic">nisi</hi>, except that, = only: “only I am redeemer,” equivalent to, assuredly I am redeemer (cf. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §356, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). Consequently there is no reason whatever for removing the אם from the text, as the Masorites have done (in the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>).<note placement="foot">What the ל <hi type="italic">maju sc.</hi>, in ליני signifies, is uncertain. According to the smaller Masora, it was only found among the eastern (i.e., Palestinian) Jews. Consequently <hi type="italic">Hiller</hi> (in his Arcanum <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> et Ctibh, p. 163) conjectures that they used it to point out a various reading, viz., that לנּי should be the reading here. But this is hardly correct.</note> <div eID="gen3594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3595" type="x-p"/> Ruth was to lie till morning, because she could not easily return to the city in the dark at midnight; but, as is shown in Rth 3:14, she did not stay till actual daybreak, but “<hi type="italic">before one could know another, she rose up, and he said</hi> (i.e., as Boaz had said), <hi type="italic">It must not be known that the woman came to the threshing-floor.</hi>” For this would have injured the reputation not only of Ruth, but also of Boaz himself.
entries.1c3639495509861e33c5a0c8013a7b2841165e24: Rth 3:15 <div eID="gen3595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3596" type="x-p"/> He then said, “Bring the cloak that thou hast on, and lay hold of it” (to hold it open), and measured for her six measures of barley into it as a present, that she might not to back empty to her mother-in-law (Rth 3:17). מטפּחת, here and <reference osisRef="Isa.3.22">Isa 3:22</reference>, is a broad upper garment, <hi type="italic">pallium</hi>, possibly only a large shawl. “As the cloaks worn by the ancients were so full, that one part was thrown upon the shoulder, and another gathered up under the arm, Ruth, by holding a certain part, could receive into her bosom the corn which Boaz gave her” (<hi type="italic">Schröder</hi>, De vestit. mul. p. 264). <hi type="italic">Six</hi> (measures of) <hi type="italic">barley</hi>: the measure is not given. According to the Targum and the Rabbins, it was six seahs = two ephahs. This is certainly incorrect; for Ruth would not have been able to carry that quantity of barley home. When Boaz had given her the barley he measured out, and had sent here away, he also went into the city. This is the correct rendering, as given by the <hi type="italic">Chaldee</hi>, to the words העיר ויּבא; though <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> referred the words to Ruth, but certainly without any reason, as יבא cannot stand for תּבא. This reading is no doubt found in some of the MSS, but it merely owes its origin to a mistaken interpretation of the words.
entries.c81f2a9c1afbb8843de21b5254215268cd135e1d: Rth 3:16-18 <div eID="gen3596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3597" type="x-p"/> When Ruth returned home, her mother-in-law asked her, “<hi type="italic">Who art thou?</hi>” i.e., as what person, in what circumstances dost thou come? The real meaning is, What hast thou accomplished? Whereupon she related all that the man had done (cf. Rth 3:10-14), and that he had given her six measures of barley for her mother. The Masorites have supplied אלי after אמר, as at Rth 3:5, but without any necessity. The mother-in-law drew from this the hope that Boaz would now certainly carry out the matter to the desired end. “<hi type="italic">Sit still,</hi>” i.e., remain quietly at home (see <reference osisRef="Gen.38.11">Gen 38:11</reference>), “<hi type="italic">till thou hearest how the affair turn out,</hi>” namely, whether the nearer redeemer mentioned by Boaz, or Boaz himself, would grant her the Levirate marriage. The expression “fall,” in this sense, is founded upon the idea of the falling of the lot to the ground; it is different in Ezr 7:20. “<hi type="italic">For the man will not rest unless he has carried the affair to an end this day.</hi>” כּי־אם, except that, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.22.6">Lev 22:6</reference>, etc. (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §356, <hi type="italic">b</hi>).  <chapter eID="Ruth.3"/> <div eID="gen3597" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. III.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>THEN Naomi her mother in law said unto her, My daughter, shall I not seek rest <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> A life of Rest, and Comfort, and Safety, under the Care of a good Husband. The Question supposeth an Af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmative Answer: I will seek it, as my Duty binds me.</ns0:note> for thee, that it may be well with thee?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And now, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not Boaz of our kinred, with whose maidens thou wast? Behold, he winnoweth barley to night in the threshing floor <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which was in a place covered at the top, but open else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where, whither <ns0:hi>Ruth</ns0:hi> might easily come. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 3. 8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And it shall be, when he lieth down <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To rest or sleep, as upon such occasions they used to do in those hot Countries.</ns0:note>, that thou shalt mark the place where he shall lie, and thou shalt go in <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Though <ns0:hi>Naomi</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ruth</ns0:hi> seem to be vertuous and modest Women, and their intent was Lawful and Honest; yet there seems to be a manifold Irregu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />larity in the manner of it. First, it seems to be against that Modesty, which should be eminent in that Sex, and in un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />married Persons. Secondly, Against Honesty, both because it was an injury to another Person, who was nearer akin, whose right this was; which <ns0:hi>Naomi</ns0:hi> could not be Ignorant of: and because it was a Preposterous and Precipitant Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thod, not agreeable either to the Rules of Scripture, or the Usage of well-mannered Nations, or that Decency which even Nature requires.
